verses.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill.

He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in the middle of it, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.
“Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard.
What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? Why, when I looked for it to yield grapes, did it yield wild grapes?
Now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will take away its hedge, and it will be eaten up. I will break down its wall, and it will be trampled down.
I will lay it a wasteland. It won’t be pruned nor hoed, but it will grow briers and thorns. I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain on it.”

For the vineyard of Yahweh of Armies is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for justice, but, behold, oppression; for righteousness, but, behold, a cry of distress.
Woe to those who join house to house, who lay field to field, until there is no room, and you are made to dwell alone in the middle of the land!
In my ears, Yahweh of Armies says: “Surely many houses will be desolate, even great and beautiful, unoccupied.
For ten acres  of vineyard shall yield one bath,  and a homer  of seed shall yield an ephah.”
Woe to those who rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; who stay late into the night, until wine inflames them!
The harp, lyre, tambourine, and flute, with wine, are at their feasts; but they don’t respect the work of Yahweh, neither have they considered the operation of his hands.
Therefore my people go into captivity for lack of knowledge. Their honorable men are famished, and their multitudes are parched with thirst.
Therefore Sheol  has enlarged its desire, and opened its mouth without measure; and their glory, their multitude, their pomp, and he who rejoices among them, descend into it.
So man is brought low, mankind is humbled, and the eyes of the arrogant ones are humbled;
but Yahweh of Armies is exalted in justice, and God the Holy One is sanctified in righteousness.
Then the lambs will graze as in their pasture, and strangers will eat the ruins of the rich.
Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, and wickedness as with cart rope;
Who say, “Let him make speed, let him hasten his work, that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, that we may know it!”
Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil; who put darkness for light, and light for darkness; who put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!
Woe to those who are mighty to drink wine, and champions at mixing strong drink;
who acquit the guilty for a bribe, but deny justice for the innocent!

Therefore as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as the dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust; because they have rejected the law of Yahweh of Armies, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel.

Therefore Yahweh’s anger burns against his people, and he has stretched out his hand against them, and has struck them. The mountains tremble, and their dead bodies are as refuse in the middle of the streets. For all this, his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.
He will lift up a banner to the nations from far, and he will whistle for them from the end of the earth. Behold, they will come speedily and swiftly.
No one shall be weary nor stumble among them; no one shall slumber nor sleep; neither shall the belt of their waist be untied, nor the strap of their sandals be broken:
whose arrows are sharp, and all their bows bent. Their horses’ hoofs will be like flint, and their wheels like a whirlwind.
Their roaring will be like a lioness. They will roar like young lions. Yes, they shall roar, and seize their prey and carry it off, and there will be no one to deliver.
They will roar against them in that day like the roaring of the sea. If one looks to the land behold, darkness and distress. The light is darkened in its clouds.

footnotes.content: Isaiah opens with a love song—but it's a parable that breaks the heart. The vineyard on the fruitful hill echoes Solomon's Song, yet Isaiah will turn it to a lament. Notice how he begins with tenderness: *my well beloved.* The Lord always starts with love before judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A vineyard owner does everything right: stones cleared, choicest vine planted, tower built for the watchman, wine press dug. In ancient Palestine, this was lavish care. The tragedy isn't neglect—it's faithfulness met with ingratitude. We recognize ourselves in those wild grapes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah calls on Jerusalem and Judah to judge the case themselves. The Lord invites them to be honest about the gap between His generosity and their response. There's mercy even in the summons—a chance to see it for themselves before the verdict falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What more could be done? The question is rhetorical and aching. God has withheld nothing. The answer lies not in His failure to provide, but in the soil—a heart that chooses bitter over sweet. Judgment flows from the reality of what is, not from stinginess.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the song turns: *I will tell you what I will do.* The hedge removed, the wall broken—these aren't acts of creation but withdrawal of protection. When we refuse God's care long enough, He steps back. The wild animals come not because He sends them, but because He lets them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wasteland, no pruning or hoeing, briers and thorns—the land reverts to chaos. Even the clouds are commanded not to rain. Each detail drains the life Isaiah's people took for granted. This is what covenant-breaking looks like: the soft ground of provision becomes hard and fruitless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The parable is revealed: Israel is the vineyard, Judah is God's *pleasant plant.* The Lord looked for justice and got oppression; righteousness and got a cry of distress. The pivot word is *looked*—God expects the fruit of His love to be justice and righteousness, the marks of a people shaped by Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The first of five woes: greed that swallows land until the owner dwells alone. In ancient Israel, land was family inheritance, a divine gift meant to be stewarded, not hoarded. The wealthy who accumulate field to field violate covenant and render themselves isolated, trapped in what they thought would make them secure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord Himself speaks the consequence: great, beautiful houses will be empty. Greed destroys not only community but prosperity itself. Those who grabbed land for wealth will see their mansions desolate—the inverse of all they plotted. God's judgment is often poetic: you gain everything and lose your home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten acres yield only a bath (liquid measure), a homer of seed yields just an ephah—a tenfold loss. The units are specific to Palestinian agriculture, a word-picture of collapse. Greed's harvest is scarcity. The land itself becomes a witness against injustice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The second woe: rising early to pursue strong drink, staying late to stay inflamed. The portrait is of lives organized around excess and escape, not duty or God. These people don't stumble into drunkenness—they *chase* it as their daily agenda, replacing vigilance with stupor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Harp, lyre, tambourine, flute—beautiful instruments at feasts with wine. Yet no one respects the work of the Lord or considers His hands. We see them: surrounded by joy and music, spiritually deaf. They have pleasure but no reverence, entertainment but no wonder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My people go into captivity for lack of knowledge—not ignorance, but a refusal to know the Lord. The honorable starve, multitudes are parched: consequences follow close. Isaiah diagnoses the root: a people who would not pay attention to God cannot survive what comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sheol (the grave, realm of the dead) *enlarges its desire* and opens its mouth without measure. In Canaanite imagery, Sheol is pictured as an appetite that swallows nations. Glory, multitude, pomp—all that a people thought secure—descend into darkness. Death is no respecter of rank.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Man is brought low, mankind is humbled, eyes of the arrogant humbled. This is the pattern: pride precedes ruin. Those who refuse to bend before God are bent by circumstance. There's a mercy here too—humility, even if forced, is closer to wisdom than the arrogance that precedes it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet in all judgment, the Lord is *exalted in justice* and *sanctified in righteousness.* His character remains untouched. When human pride falls, God's holiness rises in relief. This is not cruelty—it is consistency. The just Judge reveals His nature most clearly when pride must fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lambs graze in the ruins of the rich; strangers eat what the mighty built. The reversal is stark and final. What was held in iron fists falls open. A shepherd's lamb inherits what a tyrant seized. God's economy rewrites itself after pride crumbles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The third woe: those who *draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, wickedness as with cart rope.* The image is of sin deliberately, methodically pulled close, like a cart loaded and dragged. These are not accidental failures but calculated, tethered choices. They have made a rope of lies and bind themselves with it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They mock: *Let him make speed, let him hasten his work, that we may see it.* They demand that God prove Himself or stay out of their way. This is the ancient bluff of those who refuse to believe until it's too late. They want the promise but not the Promiser.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fourth woe: those who call evil good and good evil—a reversal of all moral sense. Light becomes darkness, bitter becomes sweet. This is not weakness; it's a deliberate corruption of language and thought. When a people re-names good and evil, they are lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fifth woe: wise in their own eyes, prudent in their own sight. Self-sufficiency is the fifth trap. They need no counsel, no correction, no God. The arrogance of thinking oneself wise is the beginning of all blindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mighty to drink wine, champions at mixing strong drink—excess becomes a skill to be proud of. What should shame them, they celebrate. Strength is redirected from justice to appetite. A warrior who masters only intoxication has defeated himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They acquit the guilty for a bribe, deny justice for the innocent. Corruption at the gate—the place where justice is dispensed. The judicial system becomes a market. When courts are for sale, everything built on law collapses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tongue of fire devours stubble, dry grass sinks in flame—their root becomes rottenness, blossom dust. All five woes converge into one judgment. They have rejected the law of the Lord, despised His word. Fire consumes what has no living root. This is not revenge but the reaping of what was sown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's anger burns, His hand stretched out to strike. Mountains tremble, dead lie as refuse in streets. Yet notice: *For all this, his anger is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.* Even judgment is incomplete, waiting for repentance. God's patience is severe mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A banner lifted to nations, whistle from the earth's end—the Lord summons enemies. They come speedily and swiftly. This is the external judgment: foreign armies as instruments of the Lord's will. Judah will learn that disobedience has consequences beyond the borders they thought secure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: None weary nor stumbling, none slumber nor sleep—neither belt untied nor sandal strap broken. The army is portrayed in military language precise to ancient warfare: disciplined, relentless, ready. This is the instrument of judgment: perfected for its task, unstoppable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sharp arrows, bent bows, hoofs like flint, wheels like whirlwind—the poetry accumulates vivid details of the war machine. Each image drives home: there is no escape, no breaking this force. The description is not cruelty for its own sake but a reality Judah must face: refusal to listen brings a language it cannot ignore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Roaring like a lioness, young lions roaring, seizing prey and carrying it—the predator metaphor completes. No escape, no delivery. The enemy is hunger itself, appetite incarnate. Judah will be the prey of nations it thought beneath it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Roaring like the sea, darkness and distress over the land, light darkened in clouds—Isaiah's vision closes in shadow. Readers today hear an echo of any moment when justice seems lost, when the strong prey on the weak and God's word is mocked. Yet even here, judgment is the strange mercy of a God who will not let His people be finally abandoned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
